subject: Quantitative Aptitude
description: Advanced percentage problems — percentage change formula, election problems, population growth, expenditure-savings, comparison-with-base.

questions.stem: If A's salary is 25% more than B's, then B's salary is what % LESS than A's?
questions.explanation: PERCENTAGE FLIP FORMULA: If A is x% MORE than B, then B is (x/(100+x))×100 % LESS than A. Plug x=25: B is less by (25/125)×100 = 20%. NUMERIC CHECK: let B = 100 → A = 125. B is 25 less than A → 25/125 × 100 = 20%. PARALLEL FORMULA: If A is x% LESS than B, then B is (x/(100−x))×100 % MORE than A. e.g., A is 20% less than B → B is 25% more than A. EXAMPLES: (1) Cost increased by 10% → required reduction of 10/110 × 100 = 9.09% (to restore original spending). (2) Population grew by 50% → declined by 33.33% would bring back. (3) 'Discount' problems often hide this asymmetry. KEY INSIGHT: percentages are ASYMMETRIC because the BASE changes — the bigger number is the reference for one direction, smaller for the other. PYQ FREQUENCY: this exact 'A is x% more than B...' MCQ is a SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB NTPC favorite — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 60% of votes and won by 4000 votes. Total votes cast were:
questions.explanation: Set up: Winner got 60%, Loser got 40% (assuming 2-candidate, all votes counted). Margin = 60% − 40% = 20% of total = 4000. So total = 4000 / 0.20 = 20,000 votes. Verify: 60% of 20,000 = 12,000 (winner); 40% = 8,000 (loser); margin = 4,000 ✓. KEY METHOD for election problems: (1) Identify percentages of each candidate. (2) Margin (in %) corresponds to vote-difference. (3) Total = vote-difference / margin%. VARIATIONS: (a) 'invalid votes' — subtract first to get valid votes; then apply % to valid. (b) '3 candidates' — sum to 100% (or less if some invalid); margins are between specific pairs. (c) '%age won by' — usually means margin %. INDIA ELECTION CONTEXT: Lok Sabha elections (every 5 years), 543 constituencies. Tightest margin in 2024 LS: in Mumbai North-West, won by 48 votes (re-counted). LARGEST: Modi from Varanasi 2024 won by ~1.5 lakh votes; Smriti Irani from Amethi defeated. PYQ FREQUENCY: election % problems are SSC CGL Tier 1, RRB NTPC favorites — 1× per paper.

questions.stem: A number is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. The net change is:
questions.explanation: Let original number = 100. After +20%: 120. After −20% on 120: 120 × 0.8 = 96. Net change: 100 − 96 = 4 → 4% DECREASE. KEY FORMULA: when a number is increased by x% and then decreased by x%, the NET CHANGE is always a LOSS of x²/100 %. Plug x=20: loss = 400/100 = 4%. EXAMPLES: x=10 → loss = 1%; x=25 → loss = 6.25%; x=50 → loss = 25%. WHY ALWAYS A LOSS: the second percentage applies to a LARGER base than the first, so the absolute change is bigger. SAMPLE RELATED: increase by x% then increase by y% → net = x + y + xy/100; increase by x% then decrease by y% → net = x − y − xy/100. PRICE-TAG TRAP: shopkeepers often raise then 'discount' by same % to give an illusion of fairness; customer net pays slightly less than original. SUCCESSIVE % CHANGE FORMULA: (1+a)(1+b) = 1 + a + b + ab (with a, b in decimals). PYQ FREQUENCY: x²/100 formula in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Pre — 1-2 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests recognition of standard 'increase-decrease' identity.

questions.stem: A man spends 80% of his income. If income increases by 25% and expenditure by 10%, percentage increase in savings is:
questions.explanation: Let initial INCOME = ₹100. EXPENDITURE = 80% of 100 = ₹80. SAVINGS = 100 − 80 = ₹20. NEW INCOME = 100 × 1.25 = ₹125. NEW EXPENDITURE = 80 × 1.10 = ₹88. NEW SAVINGS = 125 − 88 = ₹37. INCREASE in savings = 37 − 20 = ₹17. % INCREASE = 17/20 × 100 = 85%. KEY METHOD for income-expenditure-savings problems: (1) Set income = 100. (2) Compute initial expenditure & savings. (3) Apply percentage changes to each. (4) Compute new savings. (5) Find % increase RELATIVE TO INITIAL savings. INSIGHT: small absolute changes in expenditure can produce LARGE percentage changes in savings (because savings is much smaller than expenditure). REAL-WORLD: this is why salary hikes feel 'amplified' in disposable income; high-spending households (low savings rate) see bigger savings-% changes. PYQ FREQUENCY: income-expense % problems in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B Mains — 1-2 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests systematic algebraic-arithmetic discipline.

questions.stem: If 30% of A = 50% of B, then A:B is:
questions.explanation: Given: 30% of A = 50% of B → 0.30A = 0.50B. Cross-multiply: A/B = 0.50/0.30 = 50/30 = 5/3. So A:B = 5:3. KEY METHOD: when 'p% of A = q% of B', then A:B = q:p (inverse). NUMERIC: e.g., A = 50, B = 30 → 30% of 50 = 15; 50% of 30 = 15 ✓. INSIGHT: this is the INVERSE of 'p × A = q × B' style ratios — because percentages flip when dividing through. RELATED: 'A is x% of B' means A = (x/100)B → A:B = x:100. SAMPLE PRACTICE: 'If 40% of X = 60% of Y, find X:Y' → 60:40 = 3:2. 'If 25% of P = 75% of Q' → P:Q = 75:25 = 3:1. CONTEXTS: ratio problems often combine with mixture/alligation, ages, or proportions. WORK-RATIO: 'A is 3 times faster than B' means A:B = 3:1 (in efficiency). PYQ FREQUENCY: 'p% of A = q% of B' is a top SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre 1-mark guarantee.

questions.stem: The population of a town increases by 10% annually. If current population is 40,000, what was it 2 years ago?
questions.explanation: Apply COMPOUND-GROWTH FORMULA: Future = Past × (1 + r)^n. Equivalently: PAST = FUTURE / (1 + r)^n. Plug: r = 0.10, n = 2. PAST = 40,000 / (1.10)² = 40,000 / 1.21 ≈ 33,057.85 ≈ 33,058. EXACT METHOD: let past population be P. P × 1.10² = 40,000 → P × 1.21 = 40,000 → P = 40,000 / 1.21 ≈ 33,058. EXAM TRAP: students compute 40,000 × 0.81 (= 32,400) — INCORRECT. The reverse of GROWTH BY 10% is NOT 'reduce by 10%'; it's 'divide by 1.10' (which gives 9.09% reduction). Compound growth is MULTIPLICATIVE; reversing requires DIVISION, not subtraction. KEY METHOD: F = P × (1+r)^n (growth); P = F / (1+r)^n (reverse). EXAMPLES — 1 year back from 40K @ 10% growth: 40K/1.1 = 36,364. 5 years back: 40K/1.1^5 = 24,837. RELATED: India's annual population growth ~1% (down from 2.2% in 1980s) — slow exponential change adds up over decades. PYQ FREQUENCY: compound % growth in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: If price of sugar increases by 25%, by what % must consumption decrease so that total expenditure stays constant?
questions.explanation: FORMULA: when PRICE increases by p%, consumption must DECREASE by (p/(100+p))×100 % to keep expenditure unchanged. Plug p=25: decrease = (25/125)×100 = 20%. NUMERIC CHECK: original price ₹100/kg, consumption 1 kg → expenditure ₹100. New price = ₹125/kg. To keep expenditure ₹100, consumption = 100/125 = 0.8 kg → reduction of 20%. PARALLEL: if PRICE DECREASES by p%, consumption can INCREASE by (p/(100−p))×100 % to keep expenditure constant. e.g., price drops 20% → consumption can rise 25%. APPLICATION — INFLATION/COST OF LIVING: when fuel prices rise, drivers reduce kilometers driven; the ratio approximates this formula. CASE: 1973 OPEC OIL CRISIS — petrol prices quadrupled (300% increase) → required ~75% reduction in consumption to maintain $-spending — drove permanent shifts in fuel-efficient vehicles. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'price-consumption' inverse-% MCQs in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RBI Mains — 1-2 per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests asymmetric percentage relationships.

options.option_text: 25 — treating percentages as a simple sum

questions.explanation: 15% of 40% of 500 = 0.15 × 0.40 × 500 = 0.15 × 200 = 30. Equivalently, 6% of 500 = 30. Option A (25) is wrong — treating the expression as (15 + 10)% of 100 confuses a percentage-of-percentage with a plain percentage. Always collapse successive percentage operators into a single multiplier: 0.15 × 0.40 = 0.06.

questions.stem: A student scores 72 marks and still fails by 8 marks. If the passing percentage is 40%, what are the total marks in the examination?

options.option_text: 150 marks as total, if passing threshold were 50%
200 marks as total, derived from passing marks formula
180 marks as total, treating 72 as the passing score
250 marks as total, based on an incorrect pass ratio

questions.explanation: Passing marks = 72 + 8 = 80. Since 40% of Total = 80, Total = 80 ÷ 0.40 = 200. Option C (180) is the most tempting error — using 72 directly as the passing mark gives 72/0.40 = 180, but 72 is the score obtained, not the passing mark. The 8-mark shortfall must be added first.

questions.stem: The length of a rectangle is increased by 20% and its breadth is decreased by 10%. What is the net percentage change in its area?

options.option_text: 10% increase, treating both changes as simply additive
8% increase, the correct net area percentage change
2% decrease, misapplying the subtraction of percentage
12% increase, overstating by treating cross-term wrong

questions.explanation: New area = 1.20 × 0.90 × original = 1.08 × original, so net change = +8%. Option A (10%) is the classic error: adding 20% − 10% = 10%, which ignores the multiplicative cross-term (−20 × 10/100 = −2%). The correct formula for combined effect = a + b + ab/100 = 20 − 10 − 2 = +8%.

questions.stem: In a class, 60% of students are boys. If 25% of boys and 40% of girls passed an examination, what percentage of the total class passed?

options.option_text: 31% of the total class cleared the examination
32.5% of total class, averaging 25% and 40% equally
30% of total class, using 50-50 gender assumption
33% of total class, rounding up the weighted result

questions.explanation: Boys = 60%, Girls = 40%. Passed = (25% × 60) + (40% × 40) = 15 + 16 = 31%. Option B (32.5%) is the most common error — a simple average of 25% and 40% = 32.5%, valid only if boys and girls were equal in number. When group sizes differ, a weighted average must be used.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above cost price and then gives two successive discounts of 10% each. What is his net profit percentage on the cost price?

options.option_text: 12% net profit, treating two 10% as a single 20% discount
13.4% net profit, using compound successive discounts
14% net profit, subtracting only one discount of 10%
21% net profit, applying discounts on cost price instead

questions.explanation: SP = CP × 1.40 × 0.90 × 0.90 = CP × 1.134, so net profit = 13.4%. Option A (12%) is the most tempting error: assuming two 10% discounts equal 20% gives SP = 1.40 × 0.80 × CP = 1.12 × CP = 12% profit. Two successive discounts compound: effective discount = 1 − (0.9 × 0.9) = 19%, not 20%.

questions.stem: A's income is 20% more than B's income, and B's income is 25% more than C's income. By what percentage is A's income more than C's income?

options.option_text: 45% more than C, obtained by simply adding 20 + 25
50% more than C, obtained by chaining the multipliers
40% more than C, by averaging the two given percentages
44% more than C, using an incorrect cross-term formula

questions.explanation: B = 1.25C and A = 1.20 × B = 1.20 × 1.25C = 1.50C. So A is 50% more than C. Option A (45%) is the classic chain-percentage trap: adding 20% + 25% = 45% is valid only when both percentages share the same base. Here the 20% is on B, which is itself already 25% above C, so the correct operation is 1.20 × 1.25 = 1.50, giving 50%.

questions.stem: A 100-litre mixture of milk and water is in the ratio 3:2. How many litres of water must be added so that water forms exactly 60% of the new mixture?

options.option_text: 40 litres of water added to reach 60% water content
50 litres of water added to reach 60% water content
60 litres of water added to reach 60% water content
25 litres of water added to reach 60% water content

questions.explanation: Milk = 60 L, Water = 40 L. Let x litres of water be added: (40 + x)/(100 + x) = 0.60 → 40 + x = 60 + 0.6x → 0.4x = 20 → x = 50. Option A (40) is wrong because adding 40 gives water = 80/140 ≈ 57.1%, not 60% — the common error is forgetting the denominator also increases. Option C (60) overshoots: 100/160 = 62.5%.
